questions.prompt: What did Ivanovsky's discovery of tobacco mosaic virus and d'Hérelle's discovery of bacteriophage have in common?

options.text: Both first saw the agent with an electron microscope before they knew it caused disease
Both found the agent in a diseased plant and then tested it on bacteria
Both passed a diseased sample through a filter that traps bacteria and found the infectious agent in the filtrate
Both grew the agent as colonies on agar plates and then tested each colony on a healthy host

questions.explanation: Ivanovsky (1892) used juice of diseased tobacco; d'Hérelle (1916) used a culture of dying bacteria. In each, the filtrate carried the agent.

questions.prompt: E. coli is about 3,000 nm long. About how many tobacco mosaic viruses (250 nm long) laid end to end would match that length?

options.text: About 1.2
About 12
About 120
About 1,200

questions.explanation: 3,000 ÷ 250 = 12. Viruses are measured in nanometers; bacteria are a few micrometers (thousands of nanometers).

options.text: SARS-CoV-2 — polyhedral capsid, non-enveloped, DNA genome
Tobacco mosaic virus — polyhedral capsid, enveloped, DNA genome
HPV — polyhedral capsid, non-enveloped (naked), DNA genome
Influenza — complex capsid with tail fibers, naked, DNA genome

questions.explanation: HPV: polyhedral, naked, DNA. SARS-CoV-2 and influenza: helical, enveloped, RNA. TMV: helical, RNA.

questions.prompt: Lysogenic conversion can be described in Module 12 terms. Which description fits?

options.text: A change in phenotype (making a toxin) rewrites the bacterium's genotype
A change in genotype with no effect on phenotype, since prophage genes are never expressed
A change in genotype (prophage genes added to the chromosome) produces a change in phenotype (e.g., making a toxin)
A loss of the bacterial chromosome, replaced entirely by the phage genome

questions.explanation: The prophage adds genes; when the host transcribes and translates some of them, its phenotype changes (scarlet fever toxin, botulism toxin).

questions.prompt: During biosynthesis, how does the host bacterium end up making phage capsid proteins?

options.text: The phage injects its own ribosomes along with its DNA, and they translate the phage genes using the host's amino acids
The host's own RNA polymerase and ribosomes transcribe and translate the phage genes, while the host also copies the phage genome
The phage genome folds directly into capsid proteins, so no transcription or translation is needed inside the host
The capsid left outside the cell is broken down by lysozyme, and its pieces are carried inside and rebuilt into new capsids

questions.explanation: Biosynthesis: phage DNA directs the synthesis of phage components by the host cell — the virus has no machinery of its own.

questions.prompt: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray crystallography helped reveal the structure of which two things covered in this course?

options.text: DNA (Photo 51, the double helix) and tobacco mosaic virus (a helical virus)
DNA and the bacterial ribosome
Tobacco mosaic virus and the bacteriophage tail fibers
Penicillin and the bacterial cell wall

questions.explanation: Module 12: Photo 51 showed DNA is a double helix. Module 15: her X-ray image of crystallized TMV showed its helical structure.

questions.prompt: Why did Ivanovsky expect to find a bacterium behind tobacco mosaic disease?

options.text: Electron microscopes had already shown bacteria inside the diseased leaves
Pasteur and Koch's germ theory (1870s) had led scientists to assume diseases were caused by bacteria
Tobacco plants were already known to carry only bacterial diseases
Viruses had been discovered earlier and ruled out as the cause

questions.explanation: The germ theory suggested diseases were caused by bacteria, so he used Koch-like methods to hunt for the bacterial cause.

questions.prompt: Which steps do the lytic and lysogenic cycles share before they diverge?

options.text: Biosynthesis and maturation — then the phage either releases or integrates
Integration and reproduction — then the phage decides whether to burst the cell
Only release — every phage bursts its host before entering the lysogenic cycle
Attachment and penetration — then the injected genome circularizes and the 'decision' is made

questions.explanation: Both begin with attachment and penetration; the genome circularizes; then it goes lytic or integrates as a prophage.

questions.prompt: Which two viruses does the lecture name as among the smallest and the largest?

options.text: Polio virus (small) and Ebola virus (large)
SARS-CoV-2 (small) and influenza (large)
Tobacco mosaic virus (small) and HPV (large)
Ebola virus (small) and polio virus (large)

questions.explanation: Most viruses are 20–1,000 nm. Lecture: some of the smallest are polio virus; some of the largest, Ebola.

questions.prompt: Why can't a phage be grown on plain agar the way Ivanovsky grew bacterial colonies?

options.text: Phages only reproduce in liquid broth, so they must be grown in tubes and can never be counted on solid plates
Plain agar contains lysozyme, which breaks down phage capsids, so a lawn of bacteria is needed to soak up the enzyme
It does grow on plain agar, but its colonies are too small to see, so a bacterial lawn is added just to make them visible
It is an obligate intracellular parasite that can only be reproduced inside a host cell — so it is grown on a lawn of bacteria, where it shows up as plaques

questions.explanation: Viruses can't reproduce on their own. Plaques are clear zones in a bacterial lawn where phages killed the cells.

questions.prompt: A single phage attaches to and penetrates a bacterium. What actually enters the cell, and why is that enough?

options.text: Only the genome — it is the set of instructions, and the host cell builds everything else
Only the tail fibers — they carry the enzymes that make new phages
The whole virus — the capsid is needed inside to protect the genome during biosynthesis
The capsid and genome — the sheath stays outside to keep the hole open

questions.explanation: The capsid, sheath, and tail fibers stay outside as an empty husk. The DNA genome is the recipe; the host supplies the machinery and materials.

questions.prompt: Which statement about classifying viruses is FALSE?

options.text: Every virus with an RNA genome is enveloped.
Viruses can be classified as helical, polyhedral, or complex.
A viral genome can be linear or circular.
A viral genome can be simple (one piece) or segmented (several pieces).
A viral genome can be single- or double-stranded, DNA or RNA.

questions.explanation: False — RNA viruses can be naked: rotavirus (dsRNA) is non-enveloped, and TMV is a naked RNA virus.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the lysogenic cycle is FALSE?

options.text: The prophage is copied into every daughter cell as the bacterium divides.
The host cell detects the prophage and stops dividing until it is removed.
Under stress, the prophage may excise itself and enter the lytic cycle (induction).
The integrated phage DNA is called a prophage.
The phage genome integrates into the bacterial chromosome by recombination.

questions.explanation: False — the host has no idea the prophage is there and reproduces normally.

questions.prompt: Compare the lytic and lysogenic cycles: what they share, where they split, the three lysogenic steps, and why lysogeny is a clever strategy for the phage.
questions.explanation: Both begin with attachment and penetration (only the genome enters, then it circularizes). Lytic: biosynthesis (host makes phage genomes and parts), maturation (assembly), and release (lysis, ~300 phages burst out). Lysogenic: (1) integration — phage DNA splices into the chromosome as a prophage; (2) reproduction — the bacterium divides normally, copying the prophage into many cells; (3) induction — when the host is stressed, the prophage excises and enters the lytic cycle. The strategy: don't kill the host right away; multiply the phage's instructions into potentially millions of cells, and if the hosts are going to die anyway, burst them and make new phages.

questions.prompt: Explain how a normally harmless bacterium can become dangerous through lysogenic conversion. Use both course examples.
questions.explanation: Lysogenic conversion is a change in a bacterium's phenotype caused by a prophage in its genome. The host doesn't make new phages, but it transcribes and translates some prophage genes, producing proteins encoded by the virus. Streptococcus pyogenes (strep throat) can cause scarlet fever only if it carries a prophage with the gene for scarlet fever toxin. Clostridium botulinum causes botulism only if it carries a prophage encoding botulism toxin. Many otherwise fairly harmless bacteria become dangerous only after being infected by such phages.
